newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Southeast Asian leaders gather for Jakarta summit.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian leaders gather for Jakarta summit.

text.p: The heads of government of 10 southeast Asian nations gathered in Jakarta for an informal summit on Saturday expected to focus on Burma's bid to join the ASEAN club of nations.

Hosted by Indonesian President Suharto, one of the world's longest-serving rulers, the summit will be attended by active and retired generals, descendants from royalty, Communist leaders and a former guerrilla chief.

President Fidel Ramos of the Philippines, Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong were among the leaders who checked into a hotel in Jakarta for the annual summit meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Also attending, for the first time, are observer nations Burma, Cambodia and Laos.
Ramos, like Suharto a former general, said on arrival the timing of granting Burma full ASEAN membership would be one of the issues to be taken up.

"We have already given that assurance (of admitting Burma)," he told reporters. "But of course, there are certain steps to be undertaken, including (setting up) common effective preferential tarriffs."
Diplomats said the leaders were expected to discuss the inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation -- the global trade regulatory body -- in Singapore next month.
Envoys to the WTO dropped efforts in Geneva on Friday to complete the text of a declaration on global commerce up to 2000, leaving it to thrash out the differences in Singapore.

After days of argument, the envoys failed to agree on such contentious topics as labour standards, investment, competition policy and textiles -- leaving the way open for a major North-South confrontation.
ASEAN states are bitterly opposed to adding what they see as non-trade items to the Singapore agenda against pressure from the United States and some other Western powers.

Burma has sought to be granted full membership in ASEAN along with Laos and Cambodia next year. But the Rangoon military government's crackdown on the pro-democracy movement of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi has led many Western nations and human rights activists to call on ASEAN to delay the move.

ASEAN has said it will not be influenced by outside pressure, but in recent weeks both Ramos and Singapore's Goh have said Burma may not yet be ready on economic grounds. Both have however stressed that the principle of granting Rangoon full membership is not in doubt.

Surrounded by the controversy, Burmese military leader General Than Shwe flew into Jakarta on Thursday. He held a meeting with Suharto on Friday at which he spoke of the internal situation in his country, Indonesian State Secretary Murdiono said. He did not elaborate.
Lao Prime Minister General Khamtay Siphandone arrived in Jakarta on Wednesday for a state visit ahead of the summit.
